policies.summary: For generating facilities proposed by a public utility or power authority, the local government must act within 90 days of a final application (120 days of a preliminary one) or the application is deemed approved, and the utility may appeal a denial or unreasonable conditions to the Public Utilities Commission, which balances local and statewide interests. Independent developers that are not utilities do not get this appeal.

Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind, solar and storage through their land use codes; the state gives them technical help and model codes but has no siting permit of its own. A public utility also needs a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Public Utilities Commission, which by statute does not decide siting, and its new plants must comply with local zoning unless it wins an appeal under 29-20-108.

Logan County, Colorado commissioners adopted Resolution 2026-4 on Feb. 17, 2026, adding Battery Energy Storage System regulations to the county Zoning Resolution, effective immediately, and making battery storage a use by special permit in the Agricultural Zone. For systems of 1 MW or more it sets a 500-foot setback from occupied structures and water wells, 70 feet from other property lines and a quarter-mile scenic highway setback, and caps noise at the state limit for industrial zones. It rescinded the battery storage part of the Resolution 2025-25 moratorium.
restrictions.long_description: applies to BESS Facilities of 1 MW nameplate capacity or more (single residential household systems excluded), added as a use by special permit in the Agricultural Zone; setback: 500 feet from occupied structures (residence, school, hospital, church or public library), and 500 feet from any occupied structure or water well (placement); 70 feet from all other property lines, 70 feet from above-ground public electric power or communication lines, 70 feet from public roads, highways or railroads; 1/4 mile (1,320 feet) from a designated scenic highway or roadway (waivable); a buffer from the property line to the fence line and another 25 feet to the BESS; the Board may waive any setback or make it more restrictive case by case; internal spacing per NFPA 855; noise limit: C.R.S. 25-12-103 levels for the zoning of the receiving property, never above the maximum for industrial zones (no dBA figure in the regulations); third-party testing before operation and quarterly, unannounced.

restrictions.description: Logan County, Colorado commissioners adopted Resolution 2026-6 on Feb. 17, 2026, amending the Solar Energy Regulations in the county Zoning Resolution, effective immediately. For solar facilities of 1 MW or more it sets a 500-foot setback from occupied structures, 70 feet from other property lines, and a quarter-mile scenic highway setback; above 2 MW it requires 8 acres of encumbered land per acre of footprint and caps footprint at 80 acres per section unless clustered; noise may not exceed the state limit for light industrial zones. It rescinded the solar part of the Resolution 2025-25 moratorium.
restrictions.long_description: applies to Solar Energy Facilities of 1 MW nameplate capacity or more, a use by special permit in the Agricultural Zone; setback: 500 feet from occupied structures (residence, school, hospital, church or public library) unless appropriate easements are secured, and 500 feet from any occupied structure or water well (placement); 70 feet from all other property lines, 70 feet from above-ground public electric power or communication lines, 70 feet from public roads, highways or railroads; 1/4 mile (1,320 feet) from a designated scenic highway or roadway (waivable); the Board may waive any setback or make it more restrictive case by case; cap on acreage: except developments of 2 MW or less, above ground footprint in a ratio of 1 acre of project to 8 acres of contiguous encumbered land held under an easement that bars further solar development for the project's life; maximum above ground footprint of 80 acres per 640-acre section unless developed in a cluster at the same 1 to 8 ratio; waivable for projects in or contiguous to land zoned Industrial; noise limit: C.R.S. 25-12-103 levels for the zoning of the receiving property, never above the maximum for light industrial zones (no dBA figure in the regulations); third-party testing before operation and quarterly, unannounced.

rows.mechanisms: setback, noise limit, cap on acreage

restrictions.description: Logan County, Colorado commissioners adopted Resolution 2026-11 on Apr. 7, 2026, 3-0, amending the Wind Energy Regulations in the county Zoning Resolution, effective immediately. For wind facilities of 1 MW or more it sets turbine setbacks of 2.5 times tip height from occupied structures and 1 times tip height from non-participating property lines, limits shadow flicker to less than one hour a year at occupied structures, and caps noise at the state limit for light industrial zones. It rescinded the wind part of the Resolution 2025-25 moratorium.
restrictions.long_description: applies to Wind Energy Facilities of 1 MW nameplate capacity or more, a use by special permit in the Agricultural Zone; setback (from the tower center): 2.5 times tip height from occupied structures (residence, school, hospital, church or public library) unless appropriate easements are secured, 1 times tip height from non-participating landowner property boundaries, 1.5 times tip height from above-ground public electric power or communication lines and from public roads, highways or railroads, 1/4 mile (1,320 feet) from a designated scenic highway or roadway (waivable); the Board may reduce or waive setbacks on sufficient justification and, where applicable, landowner consent, or make them more restrictive case by case; noise limit: C.R.S. 25-12-103 levels for the zoning of the receiving property, never above the maximum for light industrial zones at the receiving property (no dBA figure in the regulations); turbines within one mile of an occupied structure must have the most current sound reduction technology; shadow flicker: less than 1 hour a year on average at the central point of any occupied structure, waivable by the structure's owner in writing; height: subject to FAA approval (no county maximum); blade tip ground clearance at least 60 feet.

restrictions.description: In January 2024, the Mesa County Board of Commissioners approved a six-month moratorium on commercial solar projects in order to provide time to update local zoning regulations.
restrictions.long_description: In January 2024, the Mesa County Board of Commissioners approved a six-month moratorium on commercial solar projects in order to provide time to update local zoning regulations. The board approved new regulations in April 2024, ending the moratorium.

restrictions.description: In October 2022, the Montrose County Board of County Commissioners imposed a 6-month moratorium on the processing of applications for power generation facilities.
restrictions.long_description: In October 2022, the Montrose County Board of County Commissioners imposed a 6-month moratorium on the processing of applications for power generation facilities. The moratorium “does not apply to solar panels or other renewable energy components installed on private residential or commercial structures for use within the residential or commercial structure.” In April 2023, Montrose County extended the moratorium for 18 months. In December 2024, Montrose County again extended the moratorium by another 6 months.

restrictions.description: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice.
restrictions.long_description: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice. In September 2024, the Board unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium. The zoning regulations prioritize the siting of solar projects in areas that are already impacted by development. Large-scale solar projects of 30 acres or more are only permitted in certain districts and are not permitted in the Wright’s Mesa Light Industrial and Wright’s Mesa Rural Agricultural districts. Structures on solar farms are also required to be set back at least 200 feet from property lines.

restrictions.long_description: In September 2025, the Phillips County Board of County Commissioners enacted a six-month temporary moratorium on processing applications for utility-scale solar energy systems and battery energy storage systems. The moratorium applies to “utility-scale solar energy system” defined as “an electricity generating facility consisting of ground-mounted solar arrays and associated control or conversion electronics, occupying more than 5 acres and used to produce utility power to off-site customers.” The moratorium “shall end on March 30, 2026, unless terminated or extended by a resolution of the Board.”

projects.description: Primergy Solar’s proposal to build a 155-MW solar project with 155 MW of battery storage on 1,900 acres in La Plata County, Colorado has encountered opposition from a local group called Stop Hesperus Solar.
projects.long_description: Primergy Solar’s proposal to build a 155-MW solar project with 155 MW of battery storage on 1,900 acres in La Plata County, Colorado has encountered opposition from a local group called Stop Hesperus Solar. Opponents have objected to the placement of panels on agricultural land and argued that the project will cause an irreversible loss of wildlife habitat in a major migration corridor. In January 2023, the La Plata County Planning Department informed Primergy Solar that its application was incomplete, finding that the application did not include a water demand study, among other issues. The company likely will need to resubmit its application for the project.

projects.description: In December 2018, Pueblo County denied Invenergy’s application to construct a 700-acre, 100-MW solar energy generation facility with 5 MW of battery storage.
projects.long_description: In December 2018, Pueblo County denied Invenergy’s application to construct a 700-acre, 100-MW solar energy generation facility with 5 MW of battery storage. Local residents opposed the project due to concerns about fire risk, property value depreciation, and visual impacts.

projects.description: In June 2022, Empire Electric Association (EEA) began construction on a 5-MW solar project in Montezuma, Colorado.
projects.long_description: In June 2022, Empire Electric Association (EEA) began construction on a 5-MW solar project in Montezuma, Colorado. Residents fought the project, citing concerns about impacts to agricultural livelihoods and local wildlife, but they ultimately lost the battle to stop construction. Developers made certain concessions to residents, including setting the project back 50 feet from property lines, building an 8-foot-tall privacy fence around the project, and promising to plant trees when the project is finished.

projects.description: On June 9, 2022, Pueblo County denied Leeward Renewable Energy’s application to construct a 150-MW solar project on 831 acres of private land near the Comanche power plant.
projects.long_description: On June 9, 2022, Pueblo County denied Leeward Renewable Energy’s application to construct a 150-MW solar project on 831 acres of private land near the Comanche power plant. In denying the application, county commissioners cited pushback from residents and concerns about property values. County planning and development staff had also previously recommended that the application be denied due to impacts on local residents. Residents wearing matching t-shirts with stop signs cheered the decision, asserting that the project would have impeded their views of mountains and wildlife.

projects.description: In 2011, Tessera Solar withdrew its proposal to construct a 1,526-acre, 145-MW solar thermal facility in Saguache County, Colorado.
projects.long_description: In 2011, Tessera Solar withdrew its proposal to construct a 1,526-acre, 145-MW solar thermal facility in Saguache County, Colorado. The project faced organized opposition from local residents, who complained about noise, wildlife impacts, and the industrial nature of the project.

projects.description: Over 200 San Miguel community-members gathered on May 16, 2023, to discuss a proposed 110-MW OneEnergy solar farm that would be built over roughly 600 acres of land.
projects.long_description: Over 200 San Miguel community-members gathered on May 16, 2023, to discuss a proposed 110-MW OneEnergy solar farm that would be built over roughly 600 acres of land. Many voiced opposition to the project and how it could ecologically and economically impact their community. In response to this opposition, the county passed a moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects) in order to update its zoning code. In September 2024, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium.

projects.description: Cypress Creek submitted an application for the Sundance Solar and Storage Project, which would include 75 MW of solar energy and 50 MW of battery energy storage, approximately 3.5 miles north of the town of Kiowa.
projects.long_description: Cypress Creek submitted an application for the Sundance Solar and Storage Project, which would include 75 MW of solar energy and 50 MW of battery energy storage, approximately 3.5 miles north of the town of Kiowa. On April 22, 2025, the Elbert County Planning Commission voted 7-2 to deny a special use permit, citing concerns over property values and failure to meet the area’s rural design criteria. On May 14, 2025, with a vote of 2-1, the Board of County Commissioners approved the permit allowing the project to move forward. The project is expected to power approximately 15,000 homes and increase the county revenue from $16,000 to over $9.8 million over the next 40 years. Benefits of the “good neighbor commitment” by the developer include $200,000 in scholarships over the project’s lifespan and an additional $300,000 in community investments during the first three years of construction.
